new_statements.quote: In all of the Chapacuran languages for which audio recordings or reliable transcriptions are available, sentential stress occurs on the final syllable of the predicating element, before the verbal inflection (Everett & Kern 1997, Leigue Castedo 1957, Nimuendajú 1925, Weinold 2012).2 When a predicate is composed of multiple verbs forming a serial verb construction, the primary stress occurs on the final syllable of the final verb. [fn. 2:] Multisyllablic words generally receive primary lexical stress on the final syllable, e.g. [poˌɾo.naˈkon] 'his bow' in Oro Win. See Birchall (to appear) for further discussion on stress and intonation in Chapacuran languages.
new_statements.citation: Birchall, Joshua. 2018. Historical change in reported speech constructions in the Chapacuran family. Journal of Historical Linguistics 8(1): 7-30. doi:10.1075/jhl.00003.bir.

Birchall's claim is for 'all of the Chapacuran languages for which audio recordings or reliable transcriptions are available' (word-level rule in fn. 2 exemplified with Oro Win); Tora enters only through the citation of Nimuendaju 1925. Family-level generalisation, not a Tora-specific statement; reading/type follow from the text. | checker: Crossref confirms DOI 10.1075/jhl.00003.bir (Birchall 2018, JHL 8:1). new_statements.relation_note: Family-level final stress (word and sentence); nothing on tone.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Across Chapacuran (evidence base explicitly including Nimuendajú's 1925 Torá transcriptions), primary lexical stress falls on the final syllable of multisyllabic words; at sentence level the main stress falls on the final syllable of the predicating element (the last verb of a serial construction), immediately before the unstressed inflectional particle.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not described; the one transcribed example [poˌɾo.naˈkon] (Oro Win) shows a secondary stress two syllables before the final primary.
new_statements.exceptions: 'generally' (no list of exceptions); post-verbal inflectional particles are unstressed; a verbal modifier standing between predicate and particle takes the sentential stress instead of the verb (sect. 2, exx. 13-14, Oro Win).
new_statements.identity_note: Family-wide paper by the Chapacuran specialist; Torá (Moreic branch, Nimuendajú 1925 data) is one of the languages exemplified (exx. 4, 6, 9, 26, all from Nimuendajú 1925: 154-157). The stress statement is a generalisation over 'all of the Chapacuran languages for which audio recordings or reliable transcriptions are available' and explicitly lists Nimuendajú 1925 - the Torá source - among its evidence; it is therefore second-hand for Torá (read off Nimuendajú's accent marks), first-hand for Oro Win/Wari'/Moré.
